title: It's 10pm. Do You Know Where Your Agents Are? — Kim Maida, Keycard
talk_summary: Kim Maida argues that agents given broad API keys are overprivileged and act on their own judgment unsupervised, and demonstrates OAuth 2.0 token exchange (RFC 8693) with a security token service to mint short-lived, task-scoped, ephemeral tokens per tool call, gated by policy. The demo shows a policy engine blocking a database drop before any credential exists, and requiring a human approver to hold a specific role before their consent counts.

takeaways.technique: Per-tool-call scoped ephemeral credentials instead of shared API keys
takeaways.what_they_do: The runtime exchanges a subject token at a security token service for a short-lived token whose audience is only the target MCP server and whose scope covers only the current tool call; the token is never stored and is discarded after the call.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's also ephemeral meaning it should never be stored ... it discards it as soon as the call is done
takeaways.numbers: tokens expiring within a few minutes

takeaways.what_they_do: Governance policy checks requested scope, requesting agent identity, delegating user, and target resource before the token is issued, so disallowed actions never produce a usable credential.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the policy evaluates before the credential is minted, which means you don't have an overprivileged credential that's just floating around

takeaways.technique: Role-gated human approval (not just any consent)
takeaways.what_they_do: For in-between actions the agent asks the user to approve, but a second policy requires the approving human to hold a specific role; an exhausted operator without the role cannot rubber-stamp.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the human user needs to have a specific role in order to be able to do this. And I actually do not have that role

takeaways.technique: Identity chain: agent identity + on-behalf-of user + delegated scope in every audit record
takeaways.what_they_do: Every tool call carries three facts — which agent, on whose behalf, with what delegated access — so the audit log attributes actions instead of showing anonymous API-key usage.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We know the identity of the agent that's requesting access. We know the identity of the user on whose behalf is acting.

takeaways.technique: Gateway between agent runtime and downstream tools as the enforcement point
takeaways.what_they_do: An OAuth client/gateway sits between the MCP client and third-party MCP servers, so off-the-shelf CLIs and custom agents both route through one place where scopes and policy are applied.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this might be a gateway between the MCP client and a thirdparty MCP server ... or a CLI wrapper around an off-the-shelf coding agent
